title: Protective Capacity Profiles: tenant preemption, warm-up, and controlled rollouts PRD
creator: Ananya Rao
description: PRD for Protective Capacity Profiles (PCP): a tenant-facing configuration and server-side controller that lets operators define controlled preemption behaviors, warm-up policies, and staged rollouts for reserved (committed) and burst capacity. PCPs enable safer eviction of low-priority workloads, predictable warm-start behavior after preemption, and automated rollout gates for policy changes without full tenant disruption.
background: Customers on Dedicated tell us they need deterministic behavior when capacity is constrained: predictable preemption that avoids catastrophic quality drops, faster recovery after being preempted, and safer policy changes. Existing reserved pools + burst systems can evict work abruptly or force tenants to redesign job retry logic. PCPs are designed to add application-aware, observable, and operator-controllable behavior on top of existing reservation and autoscale primitives.
goals: Provide per-tenant profiles to tune preemption aggressiveness (grace windows, max in-flight requests to preempt)
Add warm-up option so preempted model containers resume with prioritized prefetch/kv-cache warming for a configurable window
Support staged rollout for profile changes with canary fraction + automatic rollback on SLO regressions
Surface clear telemetry and alerts in Console for preemption events and effectiveness of warm-up
Maintain backwards compatibility with existing reserved pool semantics and Dedicated APIs
non_goals: Replacing tenant-side retry logic or application-level backoff strategies
Building a multi-tenant scheduler from scratch (we will integrate with existing scheduler components)
Changing billing semantics for reserved/burst capacity
user_personas: Platform engineer at a customer: configures tenant policies to match SLOs and cost targets
Redwood SRE/operator: enforces cluster stability during spikes and needs observability and safe rollback
Product engineer building an LLM endpoint: needs predictable latency and recovery after preemption
success_metrics: Reduction in P99 latency spike windows after preemption events by 40% for customers using PCP
<10% increase in warm-start time-to-stable-90th-token-latency compared to baseline after warm-up enabled
>70% of policy rollouts succeed without manual rollback when using canary gating
Operator time spent debugging capacity preemption incidents reduced by 30% (tracked via playbook run counts)
requirements: Config model: allow PCP objects bound to tenant or pool with fields: preemption_mode (immediate|graceful|defer), grace_seconds (int), preempt_fraction (0-1), max_preempt_concurrent (int), warmup_enabled (bool), warmup_window_seconds (int), warmup_priority_boost (0-100)
Server-side enforcement: scheduler must consult PCP before evicting in-flight requests or model containers
Warm-up mechanism: controller to instruct prewarmed KV-cache and prioritized token-prefetch for affected model instances. Must be rate-limited and observable
Rollout controller: support canary fraction (0-1), canary_duration_seconds, rollback_on_slo_thresholds (latency_pct_over_baseline), and manual abort
API/Console: create/edit PCP, preview estimated impact using recent traffic profile, and a dry-run mode
Telemetry: emit structured events for preemption_decision, warmup_start/complete, rollout_step, rollback_trigger with tenant id, profile id, and preemption outcomes
Compatibility: operate with reserved pools and burst policies; fall back to default behavior if PCP is absent
Failure modes: controller must have safe defaults (no preemption) if its datastore is unavailable
api_changes: Add /v1/tenants/{id}/capacity_profiles endpoints (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE) and /v1/admin/rollouts to control staged changes. Add profile reference in existing reserved pool and autoscale configuration objects.
acceptance_criteria: Operators can create and attach a PCP to a tenant via API and Console
When preemption is triggered under constrained capacity, the scheduler uses profile parameters (grace_seconds, preempt_fraction, max_preempt_concurrent) to select evictions
Warm-up flow executes: after a preemption-triggered scale-up, warmup_start event is emitted, prioritized cache-prefetch occurs, and warmup_complete is emitted within warmup_window_seconds
Canary rollout: profile change can be deployed to 5% of traffic for a configurable window and automatically rollback if P95 latency for canary > 2x baseline
Telemetry for preemption and rollouts is visible in Console with per-tenant filters and can be exported to customer telemetry destinations
Controllers have documented safe defaults and behave as no-op if downstream services (datastore/agent) are unreachable
Comprehensive e2e tests demonstrate correct behavior under synthetic spike scenarios and are included in CI
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (internal alpha, 2 weeks): implement API, backend enforcement, and basic warm-up; expose to SRE and two pilot tenants
Phase 2 (private beta, 6 weeks): Console integration, telemetry dashboards, canary rollout controller, and broader tenant pilot (5 customers)
Phase 3 (GA, 4 weeks): Documentation, support playbook, default profiles library, and migration path for existing reserved pools
Post-GA (ongoing): add advanced tuning suggestions in Optimize and integrate into Dedicated autoscale recommendations
monitoring_and_sla: Track preemption_event_rate, warmup_success_rate, rollout_rollback_rate, and tenant_p99_latency_post_preemption. Alerts: rollout_rollback_rate > 5% in 1h; warmup_success_rate < 90% for a tenant. Documented SLOs will be part of dedicated-2026.2 SLA addendum.
migration_plan: Provide a one-click migration that can associate existing reserved pools with a default PCP (graceful). Offer dry-run report showing estimated preemption behavior. Customers can opt-out to retain legacy behavior.
risks: Warm-up may increase short-term token cost by prefetching; customers need visibility and opt-out
Incorrect preemption parameters could cause larger-than-needed evictions — mitigate with conservative defaults and canary gating
Controller bugs could cause false rollback or silent no-op — require feature flags and observability
Complexity of API may confuse customers; require guided defaults and templates
open_questions: Should warm-up be billed as a separate token-cost bucket or included in existing requests?
What is the recommended default for warmup_priority_boost across model classes (causal vs. encoder-decoder)?
Do we expose an advanced tuning console for per-route profiles or limit to tenant-level first?
What guardrails should we place on max_preempt_concurrent to prevent cascading evictions?
